readingPassages.title: Part A: NO MORE CLASSES
readingPassages.content: The use of computers has meant students can study language programmes in their own speed when and for how long they want. What's more, in the virtual classrooms of the future the student will (1) ........ on their headset, and be transported into an imaginary school, choose their class, take the books they need off the shelf and (2) ........ conversations with other computerized students. They might (3) ........ choose to pay a visit to the supermarket or the train station, the bank or the restaurant. At the (4) ........ of a button they would be transported to (5) ........ realistic settings where they could practice their English, maybe getting a hand from a virtual English companion. All this perhaps, at the computer, from the comfort of their home: no (6) ........ to catch the bus to college, or ride a bike to schools. Exciting? Certainly, and an interesting alternative to traditional classroom lessons. But would it ever (7) ........ the classroom? Hopefully not. Surely the need to relate to real people talking about real issues and generally learning a little more about others will always lead language learners to (8) ........ at least a little of their time with real people.

readingPassages.title: Part B: WORKING AND LIVING IN A DIFFERENT COUNTRY
readingPassages.content:
Yearnings for the bamboo forests of China, the ski slopes of Switzerland and the karaoke booths of Japan – highlights of my previous gap years – don't surprise me, but I never imagined the minarets of Saudi Arabia would call me back. It is two years since I returned from Jeddah, but when I close my eyes on a grey English day I'm walking the city's ancient streets again, seeking out Bukhari chicken or Egyptian flat bread.

Money was my motivation for going to a country famous for exporting oil; it has some of the best paid English teaching jobs in the world, and I managed to save £8,500 in just six months working at a boys' school there. I chose my new home city carefully. As the gateway to Mecca, through which the Muslim world passes on the hajj, the port of Jeddah is Saudi Arabia's most cosmopolitan and liberal city.

My new Saudi friends warned me against even visiting the capital Riyadh, home of Wahhabism. In Jeddah I knew Saudis, as well as western women, who walked the streets unaccompanied by a man and with their heads uncovered, something they could never do in Riyadh.

Jeddah also boasts some of the world's best coral reefs. Diving on the Saudi side of the Red Sea offers the same underwater riches as the Egyptian Sinai, but without the crowds. On the downside, I didn't speak to a woman for my first two months there, but I eventually found a private beach where the sexes could mix.

readingPassages.title: Part C: FASHION DURING RECESSION
readingPassages.content:
Current economic trends present an opportunity for many people to look at fashion in a way they haven’t before. Many consumers are looking for fashion that is not only affordable, but stylish as well. According to some fashion experts, this has forced designers and retailers to lose the excess fluff and get back to the meat and potatoes of their lines and offerings. That can mean clothes with a better fit and designs that are more in tune with their target markets, says Amanda Lovell, department chair of Fashion Design at The Art Institute of New York City. “By making less and offering less, there is a stronger focus on producing items that are known sellers,” Lovell says. “Designers and retailers need to get the most out of every purchase a customer makes, due to the fact that customers are thinking twice before buying excess pieces.”

Each fashion brand, designer, and retailer has items that are known sellers, Lovell explains. “For example, the Gap most likely sells their short sleeve Crewneck or V-neck, black fitted T-shirts for both men and women season after season regardless of the economy or forces in the trend cycle,” she offers. Designers also have responded by offering lower-priced bridge lines, adds Mary Hall, who provides money-saving tips on fashion, dining out, and entertainment in her blog The Recessionista. “There are fewer and fewer high-end collections with high prices coming out,” says Hall, a Los Angeles marketing manager. “Now we have Norma Kamali at Walmart, Vera Wang and Dana Buchman at Kohl’s, and the annual H&M designers. It makes fashion so much more accessible to consumers.”

And as fashion focuses on getting more bang for the buck, shoppers are on the hunt for versatile clothing items that have a long shelf life. We all just got a little wiser and started buying classic clothes that last longer.

readingPassages.title: Part D: BURGLARY AND HOW TO AVOID IT
readingPassages.content:
A well-protected home is far less likely to be burgled than one with poor security. Most intruders are opportunists who look for an easy target. If your house appears occupied and difficult to break into, they will simply move on to an easier prospect.

Never leave a spare key under the doormat or in a flower pot outside your front door; these are the very first places any burglar will check. Furthermore, ensure that small windows, especially those near door locks, are properly secured. Many homeowners mistakenly believe that small fanlight windows are too narrow for someone to crawl through, but experienced burglars can gain entry through remarkably small openings.

Investing in sturdy window locks, deadbolts, and an intruder alarm system is money very well spent. Install a burglar alarm if you can afford it as another strong line of defense. Remember that not all criminals force their way into a home: bogus callers pretending to be water or gas inspectors often trick vulnerable or elderly residents into opening the door. Fitting a safety chain and an eye-hole viewer allows you to inspect callers before letting anyone in. If you wake at night and hear an intruder inside, never confront them directly; lock your room door, call the emergency services, and wait for the police.

readingPassages.title: Part E: THE CONCEPT OF TIME
readingPassages.content:
If you can read a clock, you can know the time of day. But no one knows what time itself is. We cannot see it. We cannot touch it. We cannot hear it. We know it only by the way we mark its passing. For all our success in measuring the smallest parts of time, time remains one of the great mysteries of the universe. One way to think about time is to imagine a world without time. There could be no movement, because time and movement cannot be separated. A world without time could exist only as long as there were no changes. For time and change are linked. We know that time has passed when something changes.

In the real world, the world with time, changes never stop. Some changes happen only once in a while, like an eclipse of the moon. Others happen repeatedly, like the rising and setting of the sun. Humans always have noted natural events that repeat themselves. When people began to count such events, they began to measure time. In early human history, the only changes that seemed to repeat themselves evenly were the movements of objects in the sky. The most easily seen result of these movements was the difference between light and darkness.

The sun rises in the eastern sky, producing light. It moves across the sky and sinks in the west, causing darkness. The appearance and disappearance of the sun was even and unfailing. The periods of light and darkness it created were the first accepted periods of time. We have named each period of light and darkness: one day.

People saw the sun rise higher in the sky during the summer than in winter. They counted the days that passed from the sun's highest position until it returned to that position. They counted three hundred and sixty-five days. We now know that is the time Earth takes to move once around the sun. We call this period of time a year.

readingPassages.title: Part F: THE VALUES OF BEES
readingPassages.content:
Some people might be frightened of bees, but farmers certainly know what a valuable role they play in nature. Pollen is a powder, produced by plants, that may be carried to other plants of the same type by the wind or by insects. There, the pollen fertilizes the plant, which means that it enables the plant to produce seeds. Bees collect pollen and nectar from plants to feed their young and, in doing so, they take it to other plants. Farmers and plant lovers therefore consider bees to be invaluable. Of course, bees benefit from plants, since the pollen and nectar are what they eat. In turn, people take advantage of bees.

For thousands of years, people have encouraged bees to live near them. Beeswax, the substance that bees produce to build the hives they live in, is used to make candles, furniture polish and lipstick, and it can be used for waterproofing cloth. The honey that bees make from nectar is a sweet, energy-rich food for which people will pay a lot of money. Indeed, having a jar of honey used to be a sign of great wealth. Beekeepers value their bees not only for their honey and wax, but also for royal jelly. Bees produce this to feed their young in their earliest stage (as 'larvae'). Royal jelly is particularly rich in vitamins and proteins, so it is also of great value to people with certain health problems. Honey is also thought to have health benefits, and it is often used in cough syrups and some other medicines. For all these reasons, beekeeping is an important activity.

However, some of us are not happy to see bees buzzing around. Indeed, it can make sense to fear being stung by a bee because some people, who are allergic to bee stings, can be killed by the poison in a sting. For most of us, however, it is a painful experience, but nothing more serious. It is important to remember that bees only sting to defend themselves: a bee loses its sting the first time it is used, and then it dies. Only female bees (worker bees) have stings.

readingPassages.title: Part G: CAR FREE CITIES
readingPassages.content:
Have you ever tried to get into or out of the center of any big city in the rush hour? It is never easy. The options are less than enticing: sit in your car for hours, get choked with pollution on the pavement, squeeze onto public transport or cycle, with the added stimulus of being target practice for motorists. I am beginning to think that the industrialized nations made a terrible mistake when they turned to the private motor vehicle as an instrument of improved urban mobility. The car brought with it many unforeseen consequences for urban life and is the cause of a plethora of serious problems. Our cars cause air pollution, foster urban sprawl, slaughter thousands every year, waste energy and natural resources, and exacerbate global warming. The state of the global environment seems ever more perilous as the developing world seems eager to adopt Western patterns of car use. They should be aware of the financial, social and environmental costs and encouraged to think about better solutions.

Whilst developed nations cannot deny developing nations the use of technology and resources that they have enjoyed for so long themselves, they must surely take a lead in encouraging the design and building of car-free cities everywhere. The problem is that private use of the internal combustion engine in urban centers will only be supplanted if a better option is available. What would happen if we designed a city without cars? Would anyone want to live or, perhaps more pertinently, work in it? Does it make social and economic sense? Is it possible to be free of the automobile while retaining the speed and mobility it offers? Public transport is typically a disagreeable and slow alternative to the car. It needs to become a pleasant, or at least efficient, experience, getting you to your destination more swiftly than private transport ploughing through congested streets ever could. This can be achieved using proven technology and ideas. Some cities have already banned cars, at least for some parts of the day and at weekends. We should strive for the atmosphere of a city such as Venice, which is an oasis of peace: a city without cars.

questions.prompt: Maria is interested in studying the effects of peer pressure because...

options.text: it causes teenagers a lot of problems
very few people have studied the topic

questions.audioScript:
Host: Maria, welcome. What drew you into researching teenage peer pressure?
Maria: Well, academic papers discuss it, but for me, it was deeply personal. When I was fourteen, I experienced intense peer pressure that changed my choices, so I wanted to understand its psychological root.

questions.prompt: Maria found that teenagers influence each other most strongly in...
questions.explanation: Berdasarkan riset Maria, pengaruh terbesar teman sebaya terlihat pada sikap dan tingkah laku (behavior).
questions.audioScript:
Host: In what area do teens exert the strongest pull on each other?
Maria: While fashion and clothing choices are visible, our data showed that day-to-day behavior—how teens react, take risks, and treat others—is where peer influence is overwhelmingly most powerful.

questions.prompt: Maria says that the best way for teenagers to deal with negative peer pressure is to...

ask somebody older than you for help
argue with the people putting pressure on you

questions.audioScript: Maria: Getting into aggressive arguments rarely works. The most resilient teens simply step back, ignore the toxic expectations, and actively seek out new friends who share their positive values.

questions.prompt: If asked to do something wrong, Maria thinks you should...

options.text: think about what the possible long-term results will be

questions.explanation: Maria menekankan pentingnya berhenti sejenak untuk memikirkan dampak dan konsekuensi masa depan sebelum mengambil tindakan yang keliru.

questions.audioScript:
Host: In your case study about Tom, what went wrong?
Maria: Tom kept everything bottled up out of fear. In reality, speaking openly with his parents from day one would have given him the protective support network he desperately needed.

questions.prompt: Maria believes a peer group can be a remarkably positive influence when...

options.text: they all choose to work hard and support each other at school
they have a good relationship with each other

questions.audioScript: Maria: Peer pressure isn't inherently evil. When a group of motivated friends encourage one another to study diligently, exercise, and pursue goals, peer momentum produces extraordinary positive results.

questions.prompt: Companies use films and television to market products because...

options.text: they are watched simultaneously by millions of potential consumers

questions.explanation: Media televisi dan film menjangkau audiens masal berjumlah jutaan orang dalam satu penayangan.
questions.audioScript:
Host: Why do multinational brands invest so heavily in movies and television?
Expert: Scale and emotional impact. A prime-time broadcast or blockbuster film reaches millions of diverse consumers simultaneously while they are completely absorbed in the storyline.

questions.prompt: According to the interview, films and cinema are particularly effective for marketing...

options.text: luxury watches and aspirational lifestyle goods

questions.explanation: Film layar lebar sangat efektif untuk produk barang mewah (seperti jam tangan mahal) karena membangun citra prestise.
questions.audioScript: Expert: Cinema excels at building aspiration. Luxury timepieces, high-end sports cars, and premium fragrances benefit immensely from being seamlessly integrated into slick, glamorous hero characters.

questions.prompt: Television programs and daytime serials are best for selling household items like...
questions.explanation: Program televisi harian sangat efektif mengiklankan barang kebutuhan pokok rumah tangga seperti sabun dan deterjen.
questions.audioScript: Expert: Daytime TV commercials remain the undisputed powerhouse for everyday fast-moving consumer goods—things like laundry detergent, hand soap, breakfast cereal, and basic household cleaners.

questions.prompt: Compared to traditional print advertising, prominent TV promotion can increase product sales by as much as...
questions.explanation: Narasumber mengutip data bahwa kampanye TV yang viral dapat melesatkan angka penjualan hingga 800%.
questions.audioScript: Expert: The sales spikes can be staggering. While standard print ads might nudge sales by ten to twenty percent, a well-timed television feature has been documented to boost sales volume by up to eight hundred percent within days.

questions.prompt: A popular TV show featuring celebrity chef Jamie Oliver dramatically increased retail sales of...

options.text: specialized kitchen equipment and fresh cookware

questions.explanation: Acara memasak Jamie Oliver secara terbukti meningkatkan penjualan perlengkapan dapur dan wajan berkualitas tinggi.
questions.audioScript: Expert: Take celebrity chef Jamie Oliver as an example. When his cooking series highlighted specific griddle pans and professional kitchen utensils, retail stores across the country reported record-breaking sales of culinary equipment.

questions.prompt: Most global brands partner with celebrities because...

options.text: they possess extraordinary persuasive power and familiarity

questions.explanation: Selebriti memiliki daya persuasi tinggi dan kedekatan emosional dengan audiens konsumen.
questions.audioScript: Expert: Celebrities establish an immediate parasocial connection. Consumers trust familiar faces, and stars have an uncanny persuasive ability to validate that a product is desirable, trustworthy, and trendy.

questions.prompt: Celebrity endorsements influence consumers to do all of the following EXCEPT...

options.text: develop an aspirational fantasy around the brand
pay a premium price for the endorsed item
take compulsory selfies at every store counter

questions.explanation: Teks menyebutkan pengaruh selebriti menciptakan fantasi gaya hidup dan kesediaan membayar lebih mahal, tetapi BUKAN kewajiban berfoto selfie di kasir toko.
questions.audioScript: Expert: Endorsements make shoppers project themselves into a glamorous fantasy and gladly pay higher prices. However, it certainly doesn't compel people to stand around taking selfies at retail cash registers!

questions.prompt: Famous actors and public figures actively enjoy advertising products because...

options.text: they earn substantial revenue and elevate their public visibility
they are contractually required to do so by government law
both their fame and access to high-profile film roles can increase

questions.explanation: Bintang film menyukai kontrak iklan karena meningkatkan pendapatan, kepopuleran publik, dan memperbesar peluang tawaran proyek film besar berikutnya.
questions.audioScript: Expert: It's mutually beneficial. Top actors earn millions, keep their faces visible during gaps between movie releases, and maintain the cultural momentum needed to secure future leading roles.

questions.prompt: When selecting a celebrity endorser, a brand's most critical consideration must be...

options.text: strictly choosing the cheapest available person
evaluating whether the celebrity's public persona authentically matches the product image
asking the celebrity to write the marketing strategy

questions.explanation: Kesesuaian (alignment) antara karakter pribadi selebriti dengan identitas merek adalah faktor penentu terpenting.
questions.audioScript: Expert: The absolute rule is brand congruence. A company must rigorously examine whether the celebrity's values, personality, and public perception match the core identity and audience of the product.

questions.prompt: Why are world-class sports stars and prominent actors particularly effective at driving consumer sales?

options.text: because people genuinely admire their discipline, talent, and success
because they never leave their private homes
because they never appear in news headlines

questions.explanation: Masyarakat dan konsumen mengagumi kerja keras, dedikasi, serta pencapaian prestasi mereka, sehingga rekomendasi mereka sangat dipercaya.
questions.audioScript: Expert: Athletes and top actors embody excellence, dedication, and peak achievement. People naturally admire those qualities, making their personal recommendation immensely compelling to regular consumers.

questions.prompt: It is surprising that some people are not aware _________ the danger of making a phone call while driving.
questions.explanation: Kata sifat 'aware' selalu berpasangan dengan preposisi 'of' (aware of the danger).

questions.prompt: People go to health centers __________________
questions.explanation: Pola causative: 'have + object + V3' (to have their health checked = memeriksakan kesehatan mereka).

questions.prompt: The shoes are exactly __________________ what I saw in the advertisement.
questions.explanation: Bentuk perbandingan kesamaan: 'the same as' (sama persis dengan).

questions.prompt: Until now, specific vaccines for coronavirus __________________
questions.explanation: Keterangan 'Until now' membutuhkan Present Perfect Tense, dan subjek jamak 'specific vaccines' membutuhkan pasif 'have not been invented'.

questions.prompt: The bomb exploded, ________________

options.text: destroys the building and everything around
destroyed the building and everything around.
to destroy the building and everything around
destroying the building and everything around

questions.explanation: Participle (-ing) 'destroying...' berfungsi sebagai adverbial of result (akibat dari ledakan).

questions.prompt: The traditional market ____________ to be replaced with a super mall
questions.explanation: Present Perfect Passive 'has been pulled down' menyatakan kondisi pasar telah dirobohkan.

questions.prompt: During the corona pandemic, purchase order of health products has increased _______ 90%
questions.explanation: Menyatakan persentase margin kenaikan menggunakan preposisi 'by' (increased by 90%).

questions.prompt: Some of ______________ in today’s era such as Orhan Pamuk and Jostein Gaarder seem to have a unique personality
questions.explanation: Superlatif diawali definite article 'the' ('the greatest writers').

questions.prompt: Regular exercise, ______________ a healthy diet, may contribute to a greater longevity
questions.explanation: Frasa Past Participle 'combined with' menjelaskan subjek 'Regular exercise'.

questions.prompt: What _____________________ these days? I miss you so much
questions.explanation: Aktivitas yang sedang dan terus berlangsung belakangan ini: 'What have you been doing these days?'

questions.prompt: I __________________________ her since I graduated last year
questions.explanation: Klausa 'since I graduated' berpasangan dengan Present Perfect Tense ('haven't seen').

questions.prompt: There are some possible causes __________ the spread of corona virus
questions.explanation: Pasangan kata benda 'causes for the spread' (penyebab timbulnya penyebaran).

questions.prompt: You ____________ go to the ceremony if you don’t feel like it. It will be very boring anyway
questions.explanation: Modal 'don't have to' bermakna tidak perlu/tidak ada keharusan.

questions.prompt: When I came to visit him yesterday, he ______________ on the phone
questions.explanation: Past Continuous 'was talking' menyatakan aktivitas yang sedang berlangsung ketika peristiwa lain terjadi di masa lampau.

questions.prompt: He did not understand what the teacher explained and __________
questions.explanation: Elipsis negatif: 'Neither + auxiliary + subject' -> 'Neither did I'.

questions.prompt: ____________ studying harder for exams, he spent his time chatting on Twitter.
questions.explanation: Preposisi 'Instead of' bermakna alih-alih dan diikuti gerund ('Instead of studying').

questions.prompt: I prefer buying food online _____________
questions.explanation: Pola perbandingan preferensi: 'prefer [V-ing] to [V-ing]' -> 'prefer buying ... to cooking'.

questions.prompt: I went into the bathroom and saw that somebody______ the water tap open
questions.explanation: Past Perfect 'had left' menunjukkan aksi sebelum aksi masa lampau lainnya ('saw').

questions.prompt: I failed my exam last week. If only I ____________________
questions.explanation: Penyesalan masa lalu 'If only' membutuhkan Past Perfect (Subjunctive): 'had studied'.

questions.prompt: To be honest, I am extremely _________ travelling by public transport now.
questions.explanation: Kata sifat 'worried' berpasangan dengan preposisi 'about' ('worried about travelling').

questions.prompt: Children ____________ are prone to malnutrition and diseases.
questions.explanation: Reduced relative clause dari 'Children who live in poverty' menjadi 'Children living in poverty'.

questions.prompt: You could leave me the door key just in case your friend______________
questions.explanation: Klausa kondisi 'just in case' merujuk masa depan menggunakan Present Simple: 'comes'.

questions.prompt: The holiday tour that I joined last month _________
questions.explanation: Subjek 'The holiday tour' adalah hal yang menimbulkan rasa kecewa -> 'was really disappointing'.

questions.prompt: Never before have we realized the impact of corona virus _______ our life
questions.explanation: Kata benda 'impact' berpasangan dengan preposisi 'on' ('impact on our life').

questions.prompt: He ____________ very skinny but after months of work-out at the gym, he looks well-built now
questions.explanation: Bentuk 'used to be' menyatakan kebiasaan atau kondisi masa lampau yang sekarang sudah tidak lagi.

questions.prompt: There ____________ to do as we have few customers coming.
questions.explanation: Kata benda 'work' adalah uncountable (tak dapat dihitung) -> 'is not much work'.

questions.prompt: What we need is an awareness to stick together ___________ our differences.
questions.explanation: Menghubungkan kontradiksi dengan frasa benda: 'inspite of our differences'.

questions.prompt: The weather is getting hotter ______________ global warming
questions.explanation: Menyatakan sebab-akibat dengan frasa kata benda: 'due to global warming'.

questions.prompt: The membership will ______________ you to use the gym and the swimming pool six days a week
questions.explanation: Pola kata kerja: 'allow someone to do something'.

questions.prompt: She looks very pale and confused. She___________________
questions.explanation: Prediksi dengan bukti nyata saat ini: 'is going to faint'.

questions.prompt: I did not know that you were interested ___________________ tennis.
questions.explanation: Kata sifat 'interested' berpasangan dengan 'in + V-ing' ('interested in playing').

questions.prompt: What is the longest journey ______________________?
questions.explanation: Klausa penjelas: 'the longest journey you have ever made'.

questions.prompt: He apologized to me _____________ my lap top
questions.explanation: Permohonan maaf: 'apologize for having broken'.

questions.prompt: I know it is a difficult decision but if ______________, I would stay in Jakarta
questions.explanation: Conditional Type 2 untuk saran: 'if I were you'.

questions.prompt:
A: ___________________ hiring an interior designer for our new café?
B: Yes, that's a good idea.
questions.explanation: Saran dengan 'How about' diikuti gerund: 'How about hiring...?'

questions.prompt: All of the luggage __________ at the entrance
questions.explanation: Bentuk pasif modal: 'must be checked'.

questions.prompt: What is happening in the world today __________ years ago
questions.explanation: Pola infinitive: 'was difficult to imagine'.

questions.prompt: He was so happy with his daughter’s school grades ______________________

options.text: that he bought her a new laptop
and he bought her a new laptop
so that he bought her a new laptop
and so he bought her a new laptop

questions.explanation: Pola korelasi: 'so + adjective + that + clause' ('so happy that he bought...').

questions.prompt: In 2030, university education ________________ include more apprenticeship in businesses and industries.
questions.explanation: Adverb of probability diletakkan setelah modal: 'will probably include'.

questions.prompt: Having a regular exercise is good for your health. ________ eating a lot of vegetable helps our metabolism.
questions.explanation: Transisi perbandingan paralel: 'Similarly' (Demikian pula).

questions.prompt: Choose the right word for blank (1) in the reading passage: 'the student will (1) ........ on their headset'
questions.explanation: Phrasal verb yang tepat untuk memakai atau mengenakan headset/pakaian/perangkat adalah 'put on' ('put on their headset').

questions.prompt: Choose the right word for blank (2): 'and (2) ........ conversations with other computerized students'
questions.explanation: Kolokasi kata kerja yang lazim dan tepat untuk percakapan adalah 'hold conversations' (atau have conversations).

questions.prompt: Choose the right word for blank (3): 'They might (3) ........ choose to pay a visit to the supermarket'
questions.explanation: Konteks kalimat menunjukkan alternatif pilihan lain: 'They might instead choose...' (Mereka malah/alih-alih dapat memilih untuk berkunjung...).

questions.prompt: Choose the right word for blank (4): 'At the (4) ........ of a button they would be transported'
questions.explanation: Idiom bahasa Inggris yang baku adalah 'at the touch of a button' (hanya dengan menyentuh/menekan satu tombol).

questions.prompt: Choose the right word for blank (5): 'transported to (5) ........ realistic settings where they could practice'
questions.explanation: Pola penegas di depan kata sifat + kata benda jamak ('realistic settings') adalah 'such' ('such realistic settings'). 'So' digunakan jika langsung diikuti adjective tanpa noun.

questions.prompt: Choose the right word for blank (6): 'from the comfort of their home: no (6) ........ to catch the bus to college'
questions.explanation: Frasa 'no need to [verb]' berarti tidak ada kebutuhan/keharusan untuk naik bus ke kampus.

questions.prompt: Choose the right word for blank (7): 'But would it ever (7) ........ the classroom? Hopefully not.'
questions.explanation: Pertanyaan retoris teks adalah apakah teknologi virtual ini akan menggantikan ruang kelas tradisional ('replace the classroom').

questions.prompt: Choose the right word for blank (8): 'lead language learners to (8) ........ at least a little of their time with real people.'
questions.explanation: Kolokasi untuk waktu dalam bahasa Inggris adalah 'spend time' ('spend at least a little of their time with real people').

questions.prompt: Where does the writer imagine being when closing eyes on a grey English day?

options.text: In the ancient streets of Jeddah
In the Karaoke booths of Japan
In the bamboo forests of China

questions.explanation: Paragraf 1 menyatakan: 'when I close my eyes on a grey English day I'm walking the city's ancient streets again' merujuk ke Jeddah.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer choose to live in Jeddah instead of other Saudi cities?

options.text: The pay is much higher in Jeddah
The weather is always cold and rainy
The place is more cosmopolitan, liberal, and tolerant of diversity
The city is completely closed to foreign workers

questions.explanation: Paragraf 2 menyebutkan: 'the port of Jeddah is Saudi Arabia's most cosmopolitan and liberal city'.

questions.prompt: What differences does Riyadh have compared to Jeddah regarding women's customs?

options.text: Saudi have different legal rules from western women
In Riyadh, women must cover their heads and be accompanied, unlike in Jeddah
Many western women can drive freely in Riyadh
There are no schools for boys in Riyadh

questions.explanation: Paragraf 3 menyatakan bahwa di Jeddah wanita bisa berjalan tanpa ditemani pria dan tanpa penutup kepala, hal yang 'they could never do in Riyadh'.

questions.prompt: What was the writer pleased to find after some time in Jeddah?

options.text: A private beach where both men and women could mix and socialize
A direct flight back to London
An English school located in Mecca
A quiet museum with historical manuscripts

questions.explanation: Paragraf 4 menyatakan: 'I didn't speak to a woman for my first two months there, but I eventually found a private beach where the sexes could mix'.

questions.prompt: What does the word 'barred' mean in general formal English and context?
questions.explanation: Secara semantik kata 'barred' berarti dilarang, dicegah, atau tidak diizinkan masuk ('not allowed / prohibited').

questions.prompt: How does the writer describe the people and atmosphere he encountered?

options.text: Very hard to get along with

questions.explanation: Penulis menceritakan bagaimana teman-teman Saudi barunya menyambutnya dan memberikan nasihat bersahabat ('My new Saudi friends...').

questions.prompt: As designers reduce the range of excess products during a recession, they...

options.text: increase the price consumers have to pay
focus on producing items that are known sellers and better fitting
close all retail outlets in New York

questions.explanation: Amanda Lovell menjelaskan: 'By making less and offering less, there is a stronger focus on producing items that are known sellers... clothes with a better fit'.

questions.prompt: As the number of high-end, highly-priced collections decreases in luxury boutiques,

options.text: fashion becomes much more accessible to mainstream consumers through affordable lines
people worry less about the quality of materials
fewer people buy t-shirts at the Gap
fashion magazines go completely out of business

questions.explanation: Mary Hall menyatakan bahwa desainer bekerja sama dengan Walmart, Kohl's, H&M: 'It makes fashion so much more accessible to consumers.'

questions.prompt: As consumers think more carefully about each purchase, they tend to...

options.text: limit themselves to only one piece of clothing per year
spend more money on trendy disposable fast fashion
hunt for versatile clothing items that have a long shelf life

questions.explanation: Paragraf terakhir menyatakan: 'shoppers are on the hunt for versatile clothing items that have a long shelf life... buying classic clothes that last longer.'

questions.prompt: According to economic fashion trends, it has become popular to...

options.text: restyle, modify, and get creative with existing clothes
purchase only vintage clothes from Paris
stop wearing shoes in informal settings
wear business suits to casual events

questions.explanation: Tren resesi mendorong konsumen untuk lebih cerdas dan kreatif dengan pakaian yang sudah mereka miliki.

questions.prompt: Another noticeable consumer trend during economic slowdowns is to...

options.text: fix, repair, and maintain old clothes rather than discarding them

questions.explanation: Konsumen memilih untuk memanfaatkan jasa perbaikan dan merawat pakaian yang ada daripada terus membeli barang baru yang tidak perlu.

questions.prompt: Lovell believes that after the recession ends,

options.text: shoppers will keep some smarter, more mindful buying habits learned during the crisis
all department stores will permanently shut down
clothing prices will double within a week
nobody will care about quality anymore

questions.explanation: Pengalaman krisis ekonomi membentuk kesadaran berbelanja yang lebih bijak dan cermat bagi konsumen ke depannya.

questions.prompt: Fashion experts conclude that during the economic crisis,

options.text: consumers became wiser about value and bang for their buck
fashion design lost its entire cultural appeal
people stopped caring about personal appearance

questions.explanation: Teks menyimpulkan: 'We all just got a little wiser and started buying classic clothes that last longer... getting more bang for the buck.'

questions.prompt: According to the passage, a well-protected home:

options.text: is far less likely to be burgled because intruders seek easy targets
is regarded as a personal challenge by professional criminals
requires excessive maintenance that is rarely worth the cost
can only be built in secluded rural locations

questions.explanation: Paragraf 1: 'A well-protected home is far less likely to be burgled... Most intruders are opportunists who look for an easy target.'

questions.prompt: According to the author's advice on home security, homeowners should:

options.text: make their house appear occupied and avoid leaving obvious signs of absence
stay inside the house 24 hours a day without leaving
leave all windows wide open during summer nights
keep all outdoor lights turned off permanently

questions.explanation: Penulis menekankan bahwa rumah harus tampak berpenghuni dan sulit ditembus agar pencuri enggan mendekat.

questions.prompt: What does the author think about leaving a spare key under the doormat or in a flower pot?

options.text: It is a dangerously predictable place that burglars check first
It is a clever and convenient backup strategy
It is recommended for houses with multiple family members
It prevents intruders from damaging door frames

questions.explanation: Paragraf 2: 'Never leave a spare key under the doormat or in a flower pot... these are the very first places any burglar will check.'

questions.prompt: Regarding small fanlight windows, the author notes that gaining entry through them:

options.text: is completely impossible for any adult human
is not as difficult as people think, since experienced intruders can squeeze through small gaps
happens only in movies and fictional stories
is safer than leaving the front door unlocked

questions.explanation: Paragraf 2: 'Many homeowners mistakenly believe that small fanlight windows are too narrow... but experienced burglars can gain entry through remarkably small openings.'

questions.prompt: According to the author, money spent on window locks, deadbolts, and burglar alarms:

options.text: is an unnecessary waste of family finances
is money very well spent as an effective deterrent
is only needed in multi-million dollar luxury estates
does not provide any practical defense

questions.explanation: Paragraf 3: 'Investing in sturdy window locks, deadbolts, and an intruder alarm system is money very well spent.'

questions.prompt: The author advises that fitting a safety chain and an eye-hole viewer:

options.text: guarantees that a burglar can never break any window
allows residents to verify visitors and avoid letting bogus callers into the house
should only be done in commercial office buildings
is prohibited by modern building regulations

questions.explanation: Paragraf 3: 'Fitting a safety chain and an eye-hole viewer allows you to inspect callers before letting anyone in' guna menangkal 'bogus callers'.

questions.prompt: Why is time such a mysterious and difficult concept to understand?

options.text: We cannot see, touch, or hear it, and know it only through change and motion
It was only invented in the twentieth century with atomic clocks
Scientists have officially proven that time does not exist in nature
Clocks are inaccurate instruments that distort our perception

questions.explanation: Paragraf 1: 'We cannot see it. We cannot touch it. We cannot hear it. We know it only by the way we mark its passing... time and change are linked.'

questions.prompt: How were early humans first able to begin measuring time?

options.text: By tracking repetitive natural events and the movements of celestial objects in the sky
By measuring how fast ocean water evaporated
By burning candles of fixed lengths in caves
By recording their own heartbeats during exercise

questions.explanation: Paragraf 2: 'Humans always have noted natural events that repeat themselves... the movements of objects in the sky. The most easily seen result... was the difference between light and darkness.'

questions.prompt: How did early people determine the length of a full year?

options.text: By counting 365 days from the sun’s highest summer position until it returned to that same position
By multiplying twelve moon cycles by thirty days
By observing the hibernation cycles of brown bears
By calculating the average rainfall over several seasons

questions.explanation: Paragraf 4: 'They counted the days that passed from the sun's highest position until it returned to that position. They counted three hundred and sixty-five days... a year.'

questions.prompt: How did early human societies naturally define the concept of a 'month'?

options.text: The time interval between the solstices
The number of days required for the moon to complete its cycle of phases and return to the same point
The duration of seasonal migration of birds
The time required to harvest grain in the field

questions.explanation: Secara astronomis dan historis manusia purba mendefinisikan bulan berdasarkan siklus fase bulan (moon's cycle of phases).

questions.prompt: Why did the historical transition toward farming require a more precise calendar system?

options.text: So that crops could be planted and harvested at the optimal time of the year
Because livestock required hourly medication schedules
To organize sporting competitions among rival tribes
Because water mills only operated on specific weekdays

questions.explanation: Pertanian membutuhkan penanggalan yang akurat untuk mengetahui kapan musim tanam dan panen yang tepat.

questions.prompt: In the context of the passage, the word 'unfailing' in describing the sun's movements means:
questions.explanation: 'Unfailing' berarti selalu terjadi secara konsisten, teratur, dan dapat diandalkan tanpa pernah gagal ('constant and reliable').

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about pollen is TRUE according to the passage?

options.text: It is exclusively produced inside commercial agricultural greenhouses
It is an unwanted substance that damages flowering plants
It enables plants to fertilize and produce seeds for the next generation
It is composed solely of crystallized sugar droplets

questions.explanation: Paragraf 1: 'There, the pollen fertilizes the plant, which means that it enables the plant to produce seeds.'

questions.prompt: Which statement about beeswax is NOT mentioned as one of its common uses?

options.text: It is used in making candles and furniture polish
It is used as a core structural material for building bridges and houses
It can be used in cosmetics like lipstick
It can be used for waterproofing fabric and cloth

questions.explanation: Paragraf 2 menyebutkan beeswax untuk lilin, semir mebel, lipstik, dan waterproofing kain; TIDAK digunakan sebagai bahan struktural bangunan.

questions.prompt: What does the author state regarding honey?

options.text: Bees make honey from plant nectar, and historically it was a symbol of great wealth
Honey cannot be digested by human children
Honey was only discovered during the Industrial Revolution
Honey must be refrigerated immediately to prevent spoilage

questions.explanation: Paragraf 2: 'The honey that bees make from nectar is a sweet, energy-rich food... having a jar of honey used to be a sign of great wealth.'

questions.prompt: What does the passage say about 'royal jelly'?

options.text: It is rich in vitamins and proteins, making it valuable for young larvae and people with health needs
It is produced by older worker bees right before they die
It is exclusively used as an industrial lubricating oil
It is toxic to humans unless boiled for hours

questions.explanation: Paragraf 2: 'Royal jelly is particularly rich in vitamins and proteins, so it is also of great value to people with certain health problems.'

questions.prompt: Why might some individuals have a genuine, life-threatening fear of bee stings?

options.text: Severe allergic reactions to the venom in a bee sting can be fatal for sensitive people
Bee stings cause permanent paralysis in all humans
Bees carry venomous spiders inside their hives
The buzzing noise triggers heart palpitations in everyone

questions.explanation: Paragraf 3: 'some people, who are allergic to bee stings, can be killed by the poison in a sting.'

questions.prompt: According to the passage, when does a honeybee typically sting someone?

options.text: Only to defend itself or its colony when threatened, losing its sting and dying shortly after
Repeatedly for fun throughout its long life
Whenever it detects a red flower nearby
Only male drone bees sting humans

questions.explanation: Paragraf 3: 'bees only sting to defend themselves: a bee loses its sting the first time it is used, and then it dies. Only female worker bees have stings.'

questions.prompt: According to the author, the widespread adoption of the motor car in industrialized nations:

options.text: was intended primarily for short-distance town use
brought unforeseen consequences and created a plethora of urban and environmental crises
completely eliminated traffic jams in modern capital cities

questions.explanation: Paragraf 1: 'The car brought with it many unforeseen consequences for urban life and is the cause of a plethora of serious problems. Our cars cause air pollution, foster urban sprawl...'

questions.prompt: The author argues that successfully reducing private car usage in cities depends on:

options.text: completely shutting down all businesses on Mondays
banning citizens from travelling outside their residential neighborhoods
providing an efficient, pleasant, and superior public transport alternative
increasing highway speed limits to 200 km/h

questions.explanation: Paragraf 2: 'private use of the internal combustion engine in urban center will only be supplanted if a better option is available... public transport needs to become a pleasant, or at least efficient, experience.'

questions.prompt: According to the author, an ideal public transport system in modern cities:

options.text: should be slower than horse-drawn carriages to ensure maximum safety
must get commuters to their destinations more swiftly and efficiently than private cars stuck in traffic
cannot be built using any currently available engineering technology
should operate exclusively on underground waterways like Venice

questions.explanation: Paragraf 2: 'getting you to your destination more swiftly than private transport ploughing through congested streets ever could.'

title: Paket 2: Fokus Structure & Pola Kunci 450
shortDescription: Fokus penguasaan pola grammar paling sering keluar di EPT (Subject-Verb agreement, Inversion, Parallelism) serta bacaan akademik terstruktur untuk mendongkrak skor ke 450+.
targetFocus: Grammar Mastery, Campus Dialogues, Academic Reading (120 Soal Lengkap)

listeningPassages.title: Part A (Questions 1 - 30): Short Campus Dialogues
listeningPassages.script: Thirty short campus life conversations covering library schedules, course registration, dorm living, IT support, professor office hours, and study strategies.

listeningPassages.title: Part B (Questions 31 - 35): Student Thesis Discussion
listeningPassages.script: A detailed discussion between two undergraduate students on finalizing thesis topics, equipment constraints, and choosing an academic advisor.

listeningPassages.title: Part C (Questions 36 - 40): Academic Lecture on Photovoltaic Cells
listeningPassages.script: A physics and engineering lecture on how silicon semiconductor p-n junctions convert sunlight into electrical current and modern tandem cell innovations.

readingPassages.title: Passage 1: The Evolution of University Libraries in the Digital Age
readingPassages.content:
For centuries, the academic library was defined primarily by its physical collections—rows of wooden shelves lined with bound leather volumes, microfiche drawers, and card catalogs. Today, however, higher education libraries are undergoing a profound paradigm shift. The rapid expansion of high-speed internet and digital archiving has transformed university libraries from passive repositories of printed books into dynamic centers of digital collaboration and research data management.

Modern academic libraries allocate a substantial portion of their annual budgets to electronic subscriptions, granting students and faculty instant access to millions of peer-reviewed journal articles, specialized databases, and digitized historical manuscripts. This shift has democratized access to scholarly information; a researcher working in a remote dormitory or overseas field station can examine rare primary documents that once required extensive travel and special security clearances. Furthermore, libraries now offer open-access institutional repositories, allowing professors and graduate students to deposit their theses and datasets for global public retrieval.

Yet, this digital transition has not made physical library buildings obsolete. Instead, library interior spaces have been thoughtfully reimagined. Book stacks have been condensed using automated high-density storage systems, freeing up vast expanses of floor space for multimedia production suites, collaborative group study rooms, and quiet individual reading pods equipped with ergonomic furniture and power outlets. Librarians themselves have transitioned from catalogers to information literacy specialists, instructing students in critically evaluating digital sources, detecting algorithmic bias, and navigating complex copyright regulations in an era saturated with information.

readingPassages.title: Passage 2: Coral Reefs: The Rainforests of the Ocean
readingPassages.content:
Covering less than one percent of the ocean floor, coral reefs support more than twenty-five percent of all marine life, earning them the nickname 'the rainforests of the sea.' These vibrant underwater structures are not merely geological rock formations; they are complex living ecosystems built primarily by tiny, soft-bodied colonial animals known as coral polyps. As polyps grow, they secrete hard protective skeletons of calcium carbonate, which accumulate over thousands of years to form massive barrier reefs and atolls.

The extraordinary success of reef-building corals in nutrient-poor tropical waters depends upon an intimate mutualistic symbiosis with microscopic photosynthetic algae called zooxanthellae. These unicellular algae reside safely within the translucent cellular tissues of the coral polyp. In exchange for shelter and metabolic waste products like carbon dioxide and nitrogen, the zooxanthellae photosynthesize sunlight, producing oxygen and glucose that supply up to ninety percent of the coral's energy requirements. This microscopic partnership is also responsible for the dazzling spectrum of colors—from iridescent greens to vivid purples—that characterize healthy reefs.

However, this delicate equilibrium is acutely sensitive to environmental stress. When sea surface temperatures rise even one or two degrees Celsius above historical averages for prolonged periods, the coral's photosynthetic machinery is damaged. The stressed polyps respond by expelling their algal symbionts in a defensive mechanism known as coral bleaching. Deprived of their primary energy source, the translucent coral tissues reveal the stark white calcium carbonate skeleton underneath. If elevated water temperatures persist, the bleached corals starve and succumb to bacterial infections, triggering catastrophic ecosystem collapse that threatens global coastal fisheries, tourism, and coastal storm protection.

readingPassages.title: Passage 3: The Technological Dawn of Photography
readingPassages.content:
The impulse to capture an accurate visual record of the physical world dates back to antiquity, as evidenced by the camera obscura—a darkened chamber that projected an inverted optical image through a pinhole. However, it was not until the early nineteenth century that chemistry and optics converged to produce permanent photographic impressions. The breakthrough arrived in France during the 1830s through the collaborative yet competitive efforts of Joseph Nicéphore Niépce and Louis Daguerre.

In 1839, Daguerre officially unveiled the daguerreotype process to the French Academy of Sciences, sparking widespread global sensation. A daguerreotype was created by exposing a polished sheet of silver-plated copper coated with light-sensitive silver iodide fumes inside a camera. After exposure times that initially ranged from several minutes to half an hour, the latent image was developed using heated mercury vapor and stabilized with a chemical salt wash. The resulting image was astonishingly sharp and detailed, capturing microscopic textures that human painters could scarcely replicate. Nevertheless, daguerreotypes had severe practical drawbacks: each picture was a unique, delicate positive on metal that could not be reproduced as multiple copies, and the required mercury vapors were highly toxic to the photographer.

Across the English Channel, William Henry Fox Talbot devised an alternative technique known as the calotype, which utilized paper coated with silver chloride. While calotypes produced slightly softer, grainier images due to the fibrous texture of paper, they introduced an indispensable concept that would define the next century of photography: the negative-positive system. From a single translucent paper negative, an unlimited number of positive photographic prints could be produced. This reproducibility transformed photography from a solitary luxury craft into a powerful medium for mass communication, photojournalism, and democratic historical documentation.

readingPassages.title: Passage 4: The Cognitive Architecture of Habit Formation
readingPassages.content:
Why do human beings brush their teeth every morning, take the same route to university, or automatically check their phones when a chime rings? In cognitive neuroscience, these automated behaviors are known as habits—efficient mental routines encoded in the brain's basal ganglia. By converting repetitive decision-making sequences into automatic subconscious routines, the brain conserves vital cognitive bandwidth in the prefrontal cortex, which can then be reserved for complex analytical tasks, creative problem-solving, and managing unforeseen emergencies.

Psychologists have demonstrated that every habit operates according to a three-part neural framework commonly referred to as the 'habit loop': the cue, the routine, and the reward. The cue is an environmental trigger that alerts the brain to enter automatic pilot mode and indicates which habit to deploy. Cues can take various forms, such as a specific time of day, a physical location, an emotional state, or an immediately preceding action. The routine is the physical, mental, or emotional behavior performed in response to the cue. Finally, the reward is the positive reinforcement that satisfies a biological or psychological craving, signaling to the brain whether the loop is worth memorizing for future use.

Crucially, research indicates that deeply ingrained habits cannot be entirely erased from the brain; neural pathways once forged remain permanently latent within basal ganglia circuitry. Therefore, attempting to break an undesirable habit through sheer willpower alone is statistically doomed to failure, particularly under acute psychological stress. Instead, behavioral scientists recommend the 'golden rule of habit change': identify the underlying cue and the specific reward craving, and deliberately substitute a constructive, healthier routine in between. By retaining the familiar cue and delivering an equivalent reward, the neural loop is rewired without triggering cognitive fatigue.

questions.prompt: The student was not only highly intelligent _________ remarkably hardworking.
questions.explanation: Pasangan correlative conjunction yang baku adalah 'not only ... but also ...'.

questions.prompt: The newly elected student president promised to make campus facilities _________ to all students with disabilities.
questions.explanation: Pola kata kerja: 'make + object (campus facilities) + adjective (accessible)'.

questions.prompt: Astronomers believe that billions of stars exist in the Milky Way, many of _________ may harbor habitable planets.
questions.explanation: Klausa relatif non-restriktif setelah preposisi untuk benda/bintang: 'many of which'.

questions.prompt: The professor insisted that every student _________ a detailed outline before writing the final essay.
questions.explanation: Subjunctive mood: Kata kerja 'insisted that' mewajibkan kata kerja dasar (bare infinitive) tanpa 's': 'every student submit'.

questions.prompt: By the time the symposium concluded, the keynote speaker _________ for over three hours.
questions.explanation: Past Perfect Continuous: Menyatakan aktivitas berdurasi yang berlangsung sebelum peristiwa masa lampau lain ('concluded').

questions.prompt: The architectural design of the new laboratory is far superior _________ the old facility.
questions.explanation: Kata sifat komparatif serapan Latin seperti 'superior', 'inferior', 'prior' selalu berpasangan dengan 'to', bukan 'than'.

questions.prompt: Not until the final experiment was completed _________ the hypothesis could be validated.
questions.explanation: Inversion setelah frasa negatif 'Not until...': Klausa utama dibalik menjadi Auxiliary (did) + Subjek (the researchers) + V1 (realize).

questions.prompt: The (a) rapid growth of renewable energy technologies (b) have reduced reliance on (c) fossil fuels throughout (d) the country.

questions.prompt: Despite (a) she was exhausted after (b) the lengthy examination, Maria (c) continued working on her (d) graduation project.

questions.prompt: The university campus (a) includes five libraries, three cafeterias, and (b) variety modern (c) athletic facilities for (d) enrolled students.

questions.prompt: The newly published (a) textbook contains (b) comprehensive explanations, helpful diagrams, and (c) practice exercises that are (d) extreme useful.

questions.prompt: Although the new laboratory microscope (a) costs significantly more than the previous model, (b) but it provides far (c) higher image resolution (d) for research.

readingPassages.title: Passage 1: The Global History and Trade Dynamics of Coffee
readingPassages.content:
Today, coffee is one of the world's most ubiquitous beverages and the second most actively traded legal commodity globally, trailing only petroleum. Yet the story of coffee originated in the mist-shrouded highlands of Ethiopia, where wild Coffea arabica shrubs grew abundantly. According to local folklore, an Ethiopian goat herder named Kaldi first observed that his flock became remarkably energized and restless after grazing on the crimson berries of a particular wild bush. Intrigued, Kaldi presented the berries to a local monastery, where monks boiled them into a bitter brew that enabled them to stay awake during long nocturnal prayers.

From Ethiopia, coffee cultivation migrated across the Red Sea into Yemen during the fifteenth century. In the bustling port of Mocha, Sufi mystics embraced the dark brew as an aid to spiritual concentration. The Ottomans subsequently established the world's first public coffeehouses in Istanbul in the 1550s. Known as 'schools of the wise' (mekteb-i 'irfan), these establishments became vibrant epicenters of political debate, intellectual discourse, and chess, fundamentally transforming Middle Eastern urban sociability.

European merchants and colonial empires quickly recognized the immense commercial value of coffee. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the Dutch, French, and British smuggled coffee plants out of the Arab world, transplanting them to tropical colonies in Java, the Caribbean, and South America. These colonial plantations relied on brutal forced labor regimes to satisfy soaring European demand. By the twentieth century, Brazil had emerged as the world's preeminent producer, a position it maintains today alongside Vietnam and Colombia. Modern specialty coffee economics now grapples with climate vulnerability, as rising equatorial temperatures and invasive pests threaten fragile Arabica crops, prompting agricultural scientists to crossbreed climate-resilient Robusta varietals.

readingPassages.title: Passage 2: The Neurobiology of Sleep and Memory Consolidation
readingPassages.content:
For decades, sleep was viewed by early medical practitioners as a passive state of physical inertia—a simple biological shutdown designed to rest weary muscles. However, modern electroencephalography (EEG) and neuroimaging have shattered this antiquated view. Sleep is now recognized as an exquisitely organized, metabolically active neurological process essential for synaptic plasticity, biochemical detoxification, and long-term memory consolidation.

Human sleep architecture oscillates cyclically through two fundamental states: non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, repeating in roughly ninety-minute cycles. NREM sleep is further subdivided into three stages, culminating in Stage 3 slow-wave sleep (SWS). During slow-wave sleep, high-amplitude delta brain waves synchronize across the cerebral cortex. It is during this deep NREM stage that the brain initiates memory replay: the hippocampus, which serves as a temporary holding repository for daily experiences, replays newly acquired information and transfers it to the neocortex for permanent long-term storage.

In contrast, REM sleep—characterized by low-voltage, desynchronized brain waves resembling awake states, accompanied by rapid ocular movements and complete skeletal muscle paralysis—serves a distinctly different cognitive function. During REM sleep, the brain integrates newly formed memories into pre-existing associative cognitive networks. This cross-referencing fosters abstract pattern recognition, creative problem-solving, and emotional regulation, allowing individuals to extract broader conceptual meanings from raw factual data. Chronic sleep deprivation severely impedes hippocampal function, reducing the brain's ability to encode new facts by up to forty percent while allowing metabolic neurotoxic waste products, such as beta-amyloid plaques, to accumulate in brain tissue.

readingPassages.title: Passage 3: The Engineering Revolution of Offshore Wind Energy
readingPassages.content:
As the global transition away from fossil fuels accelerates, wind power has expanded from a niche alternative into a cornerstone of international clean energy grids. While onshore wind farms have proliferated across open plains and mountain passes, the most dramatic technological advances are occurring offshore. Marine environments provide profound advantages for wind energy generation: ocean winds blow significantly faster, more consistently, and with greater laminar stability than terrestrial breezes, which are heavily disrupted by topography, forests, and urban developments.

Modern offshore wind turbines are colossal feats of mechanical and materials engineering. Standing taller than a seventy-story skyscraper, the largest units boast rotor diameters exceeding two hundred and twenty meters. The turbine blades, crafted from lightweight fiberglass-reinforced epoxy composites and carbon fiber ribs, are aerodynamically contoured to maximize kinetic energy capture even in low-velocity winds. When incoming wind turns the massive blades, an internal gearbox accelerates the slow rotational speed into thousands of revolutions per minute, driving a permanent-magnet synchronous generator to produce alternating electric current.

Despite these advantages, integrating offshore wind power into terrestrial energy grids presents formidable engineering challenges. Saltwater spray is aggressively corrosive, necessitating hermetically sealed nacelles and specialized cathodic anti-corrosion coatings. Furthermore, deep oceanic waters prevent the use of traditional fixed monopile foundations driven directly into the seabed. In response, marine engineers have developed floating wind platforms anchored to the ocean floor via high-tension mooring cables. To deliver this harvested power across hundreds of kilometers to coastal cities without catastrophic transmission losses, subsea high-voltage direct current (HVDC) cables are utilized, providing the stable electrical throughput necessary to power millions of homes.

readingPassages.title: Passage 4: Vertical Forests: Reimagining Urban Ecology and Architecture
readingPassages.content:
Modern metropolises are frequently criticized as sterile concrete jungles where asphalt expanses and glass skyscrapers exacerbate air pollution, amplify summer temperatures, and isolate human inhabitants from nature. In response to this ecological crisis, visionary Italian architect Stefano Boeri pioneered a revolutionary architectural concept: the 'Bosco Verticale', or Vertical Forest. First realized in Milan in 2014, the concept consists of two residential high-rise residential towers clad not in traditional stone or metal facades, but in thousands of living trees, shrubs, and perennial flowering plants.

Transforming a multi-story building into a thriving vertical ecosystem requires sophisticated multidisciplinary engineering. Botanists and structural engineers collaborated for over three years to select plant species tailored to withstand the harsh microclimates of high-altitude balconies, where wind shear is intense and solar radiation is relentless. Deciduous trees were placed to provide cooling shade during sweltering summers while allowing warming sunlight to penetrate apartment interiors after shedding their leaves in winter. To support the immense weight of wet soil and fully grown trees, reinforced cantilevered concrete balconies were engineered with integrated safety anchoring systems. questions.explanation: Pasangan correlative conjunction untuk 'and' adalah 'both' ('both ... and ...').

questions.prompt: The university campus is much larger and more modern _________ the downtown technical institute.

readingPassages.title: Passage 1: The Amazon River Basin: Global Hydrological and Ecological Engine
readingPassages.content:
The Amazon River Basin is an ecological colossus of unrivaled proportions. Covering approximately seven million square kilometers across nine South American nations, the basin contains the world's largest tropical rainforest and discharges roughly one-fifth of the globe's total river flow into the Atlantic Ocean. The volume of water expelled by the Amazon is so colossal that it dilutes the ocean's salinity for more than one hundred and sixty kilometers offshore. This immense aquatic network is fed by thousands of tributaries originating in the glacial peaks of the Andes Mountains, winding eastward across flat, expansive lowlands toward the equator.

Biologically, the Amazon rainforest functions as Earth's premier reservoir of biodiversity. Scientists estimate that a single square kilometer of Amazonian forest can harbor over one thousand species of trees, hundreds of varieties of birds, and tens of thousands of insect species—many of which remain completely uncataloged by modern science. The dense, multi-layered forest canopy acts as a giant biological carbon sink, sequestering billions of metric tons of atmospheric carbon dioxide through photosynthetic biomass accumulation, thereby exerting a stabilizing regulatory effect on the global climate system.

Furthermore, the Amazon exerts profound control over continental weather patterns through a phenomenon known as 'flying rivers.' Through relentless transpiration, the trillions of trees within the basin pump an estimated twenty billion tons of water vapor into the atmosphere every single day—an atmospheric aerial moisture river larger than the liquid river flow below. Carried by trade winds, this vapor provides essential rainfall to agricultural regions thousands of kilometers to the south. However, extensive deforestation for cattle ranching and soybean monoculture threatens to disrupt this hydrological feedback loop, pushing the ecosystem toward an irreversible tipping point of savannization.

readingPassages.title: Passage 2: Johannes Gutenberg and the Dawn of Mass Literacy
readingPassages.content:
Prior to the mid-fifteenth century in Western Europe, the dissemination of written knowledge was an excruciatingly laborious and costly process. Every book, manuscript, and legal decree had to be hand-copied letter by letter by trained monastic scribes using quill pens and animal parchment. As a result, books were luxury possessions accessible almost exclusively to the Catholic clergy and wealthy aristocracy; an average cathedral library might house only a few hundred treasured volumes. However, around the year 1440 in Mainz, Germany, a former goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg developed a mechanical system that would shatter this information monopoly: movable metal type printing.

Gutenberg's genius lay not in inventing a single new machine, but in brilliantly synthesizing multiple existing technologies into an integrated industrial production process. He engineered a hand mold capable of rapidly casting identical, interchangeable metal type pieces from a durable alloy of lead, tin, and antimony. He formulated a specialized thick, oil-based ink that adhered smoothly to metal letters rather than beading up like water-based paints. Finally, he adapted the mechanical screw press traditionally used in agricultural wine and olive pressing to apply uniform, powerful pressure, stamping inked type evenly onto sheets of damp rag paper.

The historical impact of Gutenberg's invention was immediate and revolutionary. Between 1450 and 1500, print shops spread across two hundred and fifty European cities, producing an estimated twenty million books—more volumes than all scribes had created in the preceding millennium. By democratizing access to printed text, movable type accelerated the Protestant Reformation, enabled the rapid diffusion of experimental scientific discoveries, fostered standardized national vernacular languages, and laid the cultural foundations for modern democratic civic literacy.

readingPassages.title: Passage 3: The Physiology of Cellular Hydration and Osmoregulation
readingPassages.content:
Water is the fundamental solvent of terrestrial life, constituting approximately sixty percent of total human body mass. Within the human body, this vital fluid is partitioned between two major physiological compartments: intracellular fluid (fluid contained inside cells, representing roughly two-thirds of total body water) and extracellular fluid (blood plasma and interstitial fluid bathing the tissues). Maintaining a precise osmotic balance between these two fluid reservoirs is essential for cellular homeostasis, biochemical enzymatic reactions, and the electrical conduction of cardiac and neuronal impulses.

The human body regulates hydration through a sensitive endocrine feedback loop managed by the brain's hypothalamus. Specialized sensory cells known as osmoreceptors continuously monitor the solute concentration, or osmolality, of the blood. When blood osmolality rises even slightly due to sweating, dehydration, or high sodium intake, the hypothalamus triggers two immediate physiological responses: it induces the conscious perception of thirst, compelling fluid consumption, and signals the posterior pituitary gland to secrete antidiuretic hormone (ADH), also termed vasopressin.

Once released into the circulatory system, ADH travels to the kidneys, where it binds to epithelial receptors in the collecting ducts. This molecular binding prompts the insertion of specialized water channel proteins called aquaporins into cell membranes. These channels dramatically increase renal water permeability, allowing water that would otherwise be excreted as urine to be reabsorbed back into the bloodstream. Conversely, when an individual drinks copious amounts of water, blood osmolality drops, ADH secretion is suppressed, and the kidneys excrete diluted urine to prevent water intoxication and dangerous cellular swelling.

readingPassages.title: Passage 4: Volcanic Hotspots and the Genesis of Island Chains
readingPassages.content:
The standard geological paradigm of plate tectonics attributes the vast majority of volcanic activity to boundaries where tectonic plates either collide at subduction zones or pull apart along mid-ocean spreading ridges. However, some of Earth's most dramatic volcanic landmarks—including the Hawaiian Archipelago, the Galápagos Islands, and the Yellowstone caldera—occur thousands of kilometers away from any tectonic plate boundary. In 1963, Canadian geophysicist J. Tuzo Wilson proposed an elegant hypothesis to explain these enigmatic intraplate volcanoes: the concept of mantle plumes and volcanic hotspots.

According to mantle plume theory, a hotspot is fueled by an extraordinarily hot, narrow column of buoyant thermal material that ascends from deep within the Earth's mantle, likely originating at the core-mantle boundary nearly three thousand kilometers beneath the surface. As this rising thermal plume reaches the base of the rigid oceanic lithosphere, decompressive melting generates vast reservoirs of basaltic magma. This molten rock periodically punches through the overlying tectonic plate, erupting onto the ocean floor. Over millions of years, successive lava flows accumulate vertically, eventually breaching the sea surface to form towering volcanic shield islands.

Crucially, while the deep mantle plume remains anchored in a relatively fixed location for tens of millions of years, the overlying tectonic plate continuously creeps across it at rates of several centimeters per year. As the moving oceanic plate carries an active volcanic island away from its hotspot magma source, the volcano is severed from its fuel supply, becomes extinct, and begins to cool and subside. Meanwhile, the stationary hotspot burns through the fresh seafloor above, giving birth to a new volcanic island. This conveyor-belt mechanism produces linear, age-progressive island chains, where islands grow progressively older, more eroded, and submerged into flat-topped seamounts the further they lie from the active hotspot.
